title: What training does a California Injury and Illness Prevention Program require?
description: Title 8 section 3203: the six IIPP training triggers, supervisor training, the one-year training record and small employer exceptions, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: California Code of Regulations, title 8, section 3203 requires every California employer to keep a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program that provides training when the program is first set up, to all new employees, to employees given new assignments, when new substances, processes or equipment create a new hazard, when a new hazard becomes known, and to supervisors. Each employee's training must be documented and the record kept for at least one year.
keyTakeaways: Section 3203 has applied to every California employer since July 1, 1991; there is no headcount threshold for having a written program.
Subsection (a)(7) lists six training triggers, (A) to (F), and none of them is a fixed annual refresher; training is event driven.
Supervisors must be trained on the safety and health hazards faced by the employees under their immediate direction and control.

Training documentation must show employee name or identifier, dates, type of training and provider, and be kept for at least one year, with narrower duties for employers under 10 or under 20 employees.
Employees and their designated representatives can request the written program, which must be provided within five business days (subsection (a)(8), operative July 1, 2020).
regulator: California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA), Department of Industrial Relations; Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board (OSHSB)
appliesTo: Every employer in California covered by Cal/OSHA, from July 1, 1991
All new employees, employees moved to new job assignments, and supervisors
Smaller employers (under 10 employees, and some under 20) with reduced communication and documentation duties

sections.heading: What is the Cal/OSHA Injury and Illness Prevention Program rule?

blocks.text: It is the general safety program rule for California workplaces. Title 8, section 3203 of the California Code of Regulations, in the General Industry Safety Orders, states that "Effective July 1, 1991, every employer shall establish, implement and maintain an effective Injury and Illness Prevention Program" in writing. The rule is adopted under Labor Code section 6401.7 and enforced by Cal/OSHA, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health within the Department of Industrial Relations.

The written program must, at a minimum, name the person or persons responsible for it; set up a system for ensuring employees follow safe work practices; set up a system for two-way communication on safety, including a way for employees to report hazards without fear of reprisal; include procedures for identifying and evaluating hazards through scheduled inspections; include a procedure for investigating occupational injury and illness; set methods for correcting hazards in a timely way; provide training; and allow employee access to the program. Training is one of eight required elements, and it ties the others together, because employees cannot follow a reporting system or a safe work practice nobody has taught them.

Many other Cal/OSHA requirements plug into the program. The heat illness standards and the workplace violence prevention plan under Labor Code 6401.9 may both be written as part of the program or kept separately; see [California workplace violence prevention training](/regulations/california-workplace-violence-prevention-training) and [Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention training](/regulations/cal-osha-heat-illness-prevention-training). This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: When must training be given under section 3203(a)(7)?

blocks.text: Training is triggered by six events, not by the calendar. Subsection (a)(7) requires the program to "Provide training and instruction" in each of the circumstances below. An employer that only runs an annual safety session, with nothing at hire or at a change of assignment, is missing most of the triggers.

blocks.text: Triggers (D) and (E) mirror the inspection triggers in subsection (a)(4), which require hazard inspections when new substances, processes, procedures or equipment are introduced and when the employer learns of a new or previously unrecognized hazard. In practice, the inspection or investigation that finds a hazard should also open a training action. See [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: What does section 3203 require for supervisors?

blocks.text: Supervisors must be trained so they understand the safety and health hazards to which employees under their immediate direction and control may be exposed. The wording in (a)(7)(F) is short, but it sets a role-specific standard: a supervisor's training is defined by the hazards of the people they direct, not by a generic leadership course.

That makes supervisor training a function of the hazard assessment. A warehouse supervisor needs to know the forklift, racking and manual handling hazards of their crew; a laboratory supervisor needs the chemical and biological hazards. When a supervisor takes over a new crew, or the crew's work changes, the supervisor's training needs to change too. A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) that lists hazards by work area and links supervisors to those areas is the simplest way to show this.

sections.heading: What training records does section 3203 require, and for how long?

blocks.text: Employers must document the training required by subsection (a)(7) for each employee and keep that documentation for at least one year. Subsection (b)(2) lists the minimum content: "employee name or other identifier, training dates, type(s) of training, and training providers."

blocks.caption: Section 3203(b) record duties and exceptions
head: Record or exception
Requirement
rows: Training documentation (b)(2)
Per employee: name or identifier, dates, type of training, provider. Keep at least 1 year.
Inspection records (b)(1)
Who inspected, unsafe conditions found, corrective action. Keep at least 1 year (employers under 10 may keep only until the hazard is corrected).
Exception 1: fewer than 10 employees
May substantially comply with a log of instructions given on hazards unique to the job when first hired or assigned new duties.
Exception 2: short-service employees
Records of employees who worked less than one year need not be kept beyond employment if given to the employee at termination.
Exception 3: fewer than 20 employees

In industries not on the high-hazard list with an experience modification rate of 1.1 or less, or in listed low-hazard industries, written documentation may be limited to the responsible person, scheduled inspections, and training.
Exception 4: local government
Counties, cities, districts and similar local public entities are not required to keep records of the steps taken to implement the program.

blocks.text: One year is a floor. Because the triggers are event driven, an employee's job-specific training may date from hire several years earlier, and the record is what proves it happened. Most employers keep training records for the duration of employment so that each trigger can be shown. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How do the communication rules and small employer exceptions affect training?

blocks.text: Training also counts toward the communication element. Subsection (a)(3) requires communication "in a form readily understandable by all affected employees," and lists meetings, training programs, postings, written communications, anonymous hazard notification and labor/management safety committees as ways to comply. Employers with fewer than 10 employees may instruct employees orally in general safe work practices, with specific instruction on hazards unique to each job.

Employers that use a labor/management safety and health committee are presumed to comply with the communication element if the committee meets at least quarterly, keeps written meeting records for at least one year, reviews inspection results and injury investigations, and meets the other conditions in subsection (c). A committee that reviews investigations is also a natural place to decide when trigger (E) training is needed.

sections.heading: Can employees ask to see the program?

blocks.text: Yes. Subsection (a)(8), added with an operative date of July 1, 2020, gives employees and their designated representatives the right to examine and receive a copy of the program. The employer must provide access within five business days of the request, either as a printed copy (one free of charge) or through unobstructed electronic access on a company server or website that employees routinely use.

The copy need not include the records of steps taken to implement the program, such as training logs. Employers must also tell all employees about the right and procedure to access the program, which is a natural topic for new employee training under trigger (B).

No change to section 3203 was in formal rulemaking as at November 2026. The Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board's proposed regulations list, updated October 2026, shows notices for other sections, such as trichloroethylene, crane operator recertification and first aid, but none for the Injury and Illness Prevention Program.

blocks.title: Linked California requirements
blocks.text: Labor Code 6401.9 (workplace violence prevention, enforceable since July 1, 2024) lets employers write their plan as a stand-alone section of the IIPP, and it carries its own annual training cycle. The outdoor and indoor heat standards, sections 3395 and 3396, allow the heat plan to be included in the IIPP. Treat these as separate training obligations even when they share one document.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each IIPP training trigger as an event linked to the hazard, role and work area it affects, so a new process, an investigation finding or a transfer identifies who needs training and what it must cover. Each completion carries the fields section 3203(b)(2) requires. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Does Cal/OSHA require annual IIPP training?
faqs.a: Section 3203 does not set a fixed annual refresher. It requires training when the program is first established, for new employees, for new assignments, when new substances, processes or equipment create a new hazard, when a new hazard becomes known, and for supervisors. Other Cal/OSHA rules, such as the workplace violence statute, do set annual cycles.

faqs.q: Do small employers need a written IIPP?
faqs.a: Yes. Every employer must have a written program. Employers with fewer than 10 employees may communicate and instruct orally and may meet the training documentation duty with a log of job-specific instructions. Certain employers with fewer than 20 employees may limit written documentation to the responsible person, inspections and training.

faqs.q: What must a section 3203 training record contain?
faqs.a: Subsection (b)(2) requires the employee's name or other identifier, the training dates, the type or types of training, and the training providers, for each employee. The record must be kept for at least one year, although longer retention is common because job-specific training may date from hire.

faqs.q: Can construction employers use outside training records?
faqs.a: Note 2 to subsection (b) allows contractors licensed under the Business and Professions Code to use records of training provided through an occupational safety and health training program approved by the Division. They then need to keep records only for the steps relating to hazards specific to the employee's job duties.

factCheck.claim: Section 3203(a): effective July 1, 1991, every employer shall establish, implement and maintain an effective written IIPP; eight minimum elements (a)(1) to (a)(8).

Section 3203(a)(7)(A) to (F): training when program first established, to all new employees, to employees given new job assignments, when new substances/processes/procedures/equipment represent a new hazard, when made aware of a new or previously unrecognized hazard, and for supervisors to familiarize themselves with hazards to which employees under their immediate direction and control may be exposed.

Section 3203(b)(2): documentation of training for each employee including name or other identifier, dates, types, providers, kept at least one year; Exceptions 1 to 4 (under 10 employees log; under one year employees; under 20 employees with EMR 1.1 or less or low-hazard list; local government entities).
Section 3203(a)(3) exception for fewer than 10 employees (oral instruction); (c) committee meets not less than quarterly with records kept one year; (b)(1) inspection records kept one year.
Section 3203(a)(8): access within five business days; one printed copy free; electronic unobstructed access option; new subsections filed 3-3-2020, operative 7-1-2020; authority Labor Code 6401.7.
OSHSB proposed regulations list (October 2026) shows notices for sections 5155, 5006.1/5006.2, 1512/3400 and others, none for section 3203.
